**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Platform Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide, before the next budget cycle, whether to purchase additional GPU hardware for our local inference fleet or to invest in improving utilisation of the hardware we already own. I want to lay out the reasoning in full, because the right answer is less obvious than either "we're maxed out, buy more" or "we're wasteful, optimise first" suggests.

Start with the numbers as we understand them. Our fleet runs at roughly 38% average utilisation, but that average hides the real problem: peak-hour utilisation on our two busiest nodes exceeds 90%, while our batch and experimentation nodes sit idle most of the day. The latency complaints we've received — p99 inference times spiking from 400ms to over 2 seconds during the 9-to-6 window — are not a capacity problem in aggregate. They are a scheduling and isolation problem. We are, in effect, running a system with plenty of total capacity and none where it matters, when it matters.

That points toward utilisation work first, and the economics reinforce it. A new high-memory node, once you include networking, rack space, power, and the engineering time to integrate it, lands somewhere in the low six figures, with meaningful ongoing operating cost. The utilisation work — better request routing, workload isolation so batch jobs can't starve interactive traffic, dynamic batching, and moving our experimentation load onto a scheduled off-peak window — is roughly two engineer-months. Even if we value that time generously, it's an order of magnitude cheaper, and it attacks the actual symptom our users feel: latency, not throughput.

There's also the question of what we'd be giving up by buying hardware now. Every dollar spent on a node we may not need in six months is a dollar not spent on the evaluation work for the new model family, which is the project most likely to matter to our roadmap. Hardware purchases also carry an opportunity cost that's easy to miss: they commit us to a specific architecture. If the new model family shifts our memory or interconnect requirements — and the trend in the field suggests it will — today's purchase could be poorly matched to tomorrow's workload. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are architecture-agnostic. Better scheduling and isolation pay off regardless of what silicon we run.

Reversibility matters here too. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale. Resale markets for used accelerators are thin, depreciation is fast, and once a node is racked and provisioned there is organisational pressure to keep it busy, which historically leads to scope creep and shadow workloads rather than genuine value. Utilisation work is the opposite: it's incremental, testable, and reversible at every step. If a routing change makes latency worse, we roll it back in an afternoon. If a new node makes latency worse, we've still paid for it.

Now, the honest caveats. Our utilisation figures come from coarse instrumentation, and it's possible that what looks like a scheduling problem is actually a headroom problem — that peak demand genuinely exceeds peak capacity and no amount of clever routing fixes that. If the utilisation work stalls, or if we discover that the 90% peaks are sustained rather than bursty, the calculus changes and buying becomes the right call, probably within the quarter rather than after it. I'd also flag that our latency SLO is informal; if the product team formalises a stricter target, we should re-run this analysis against it. And there is a real risk that two engineer-months of optimisation work slips, as such work tends to, in which case we'll face this decision again with less time to deliberate.

My recommendation, then: fund the utilisation work now, with a hard checkpoint eight weeks out. If p99 latency under load hasn't improved by at least 40% by then, or if peak utilisation proves sustained above 85% across the fleet rather than concentrated on two nodes, we escalate the hardware request immediately with the data in hand. This sequencing costs us little — eight weeks is short against a hardware procurement cycle anyway — and it means that if we do buy, we buy knowing exactly what we need rather than guessing. The worst outcome isn't choosing wrong; it's spending six figures to avoid finding out whether the cheap fix would have worked.

I'm happy to walk through the instrumentation data with anyone who wants to pressure-test the utilisation numbers before we commit.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to settle a question that has come up repeatedly in the last month: should we purchase additional local GPU capacity, or should we invest in raising the utilisation of the hardware we already own? I want to lay out the reasoning as I see it, make a recommendation, and be honest about where the uncertainty lies.

The starting point is that our current fleet is not obviously underpowered — it is underused. Across our inference nodes, utilisation sits in the low thirties on average, with sharp peaks during business hours and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. That number is misleading in both directions. It understates the pressure we feel at peak, when batch queues form and interactive requests slow noticeably. But it also overstates the case for buying more, because the problem is not raw capacity so much as the shape of our demand against a rigid allocation of it. We have effectively hard-partitioned hardware across teams, so one group's idle GPUs sit unavailable to another group's queue. The cheapest capacity we can acquire is the capacity we already own and are failing to share.

That said, buying more hardware is not a strawman. There are real arguments in its favour. Latency is the strongest one. Our interactive workloads have a latency budget that we are brushing against at peak, and no amount of clever scheduling fully removes the risk that a queue forms at exactly the wrong moment. Reliability is the second argument: with more nodes, we can tolerate failures and maintenance windows without degrading service. And there is an opportunity-cost argument in the other direction — every engineering week we spend on better scheduling, batching, and shared queues is a week not spent on product work, and those weeks are not free. If the utilisation project drags on, its true cost may exceed the sticker price of a machine that simply makes the problem go away.

Against that, buying hardware has costs that are easy to underestimate. The purchase price is only the beginning; power, cooling, rack space, and the operational burden of a larger fleet all scale with it. More importantly, hardware purchases are largely irreversible at our scale. GPUs depreciate quickly, resale is imperfect, and a machine bought on the assumption that demand will grow becomes a stranded asset if that demand shifts — for instance, if model efficiency improvements let us serve the same traffic on fewer cards, which has happened twice in this space in the last eighteen months. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is mostly reversible. Scheduler changes, better batching, and pooled allocation can be unwound or adjusted cheaply, and the engineering effort invested builds knowledge that retains value even if we later buy hardware anyway.

There is also a sequencing argument. If we buy hardware now, we remove the pressure that would otherwise force us to understand our own workload properly. If we improve utilisation first, we learn what our true peak demand is, and any subsequent purchase is sized against evidence rather than anxiety. The risk is that we under-provision during the interim and degrade experience; that risk is real and is the main reason this is a close call rather than an easy one.

My recommendation is that we invest in utilisation first, with a defined scope and a hard deadline: shared queueing across teams, dynamic batching for inference, and a modest reallocation of the overnight idle window to batch workloads. I would cap this effort at roughly six weeks of engineering time. If, at the end of that period, peak latency still breaches our target or the reliability margin still feels thin, we proceed with a hardware purchase, sized using the data the utilisation work will have given us. This keeps the reversible option in front of the irreversible one, and it means that if we do buy, we buy because we measured a need, not because we assumed one.

I want to be clear about the uncertainty here. If our traffic grows faster than we expect, or if a new product commitment lands in the next quarter, the utilisation path may prove too slow and we will wish we had bought sooner. The six-week cap is designed to limit that exposure, but it cannot eliminate it. I would rather take that bounded risk than commit capital on the current evidence.

Happy to discuss; I suggest we decide by end of next week so the work can start promptly either way.

**Background**

Our four A100 nodes are now running at roughly 68% average utilisation, but that number hides a lot. Peak-hour demand pushes two of the nodes to saturation, batch queues back up, and p99 latency has drifted from 180ms to over 400ms in the last quarter. Meanwhile, overnight and weekend utilisation sits near 15%. The team that owns the recommendation-service workload has asked for two additional nodes, which would cost approximately $310K in capital plus around $45K annually in colocation and power. Before we approve that, I want to lay out why I believe the cheaper path — improving utilisation of what we already own — deserves a serious, time-boxed attempt first.

**The cost picture**

The headline purchase price understates the true cost of buying. Beyond the capital outlay, new nodes carry operational weight: more thermal load in a rack that is already near its power ceiling, additional failure surface, and the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain them. There is also a quieter cost — the opportunity cost of $310K that could fund two senior engineers for a year, or a substantial portion of the eval platform we keep deferring. Utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we already employ. The batching improvements, model quantisation, and scheduling changes we have scoped would take roughly six engineer-weeks and cost us very little in hard currency. Even if we only recover half of the idle capacity, we defer the purchase by at least two quarters, and possibly indefinitely if demand growth is slower than the roadmap assumes.

**Latency and reliability**

The counterargument deserves honest treatment. Utilisation improvements are not free in performance terms. Aggressive batching raises throughput but adds queueing delay; quantisation can shave latency but risks subtle accuracy regressions that our eval suite may not fully catch. If we push utilisation too hard, we could end up with a fleet that is nominally efficient but delivers worse p99 latency at peak — the exact symptom we are trying to fix. Reliability is the other edge: a fleet running at 90% utilisation has no headroom to absorb a node failure. Today, when a node goes down, we shed load and degrade gracefully. At high utilisation, the same failure becomes an outage. This is why I do not see utilisation work and hardware purchase as opposites, but as sequenced options: do the utilisation work first, measure honestly, and buy only what the post-improvement demand curve actually requires.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive factor for me. Buying hardware is nearly irreversible at our scale. Depreciation runs four years, the rack space is committed, and if demand shifts — a workload migrates to a hosted API, a product line is deprioritised — we are left holding sunk capital. Utilisation improvements are largely reversible: we can tune batch sizes back, revert a scheduler change, and restore the old latency profile within days. In a period where our product direction is genuinely uncertain, keeping options open has real value. The asymmetry is stark: the downside of waiting a quarter to buy is some continued peak-hour queueing pain; the downside of buying now and not needing the capacity is $310K plus four years of carrying cost.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next eight weeks on a focused utilisation programme: dynamic batching, INT8 quantisation for the two largest models where eval tolerance permits, off-peak scheduling of batch jobs, and a proper capacity dashboard so we stop arguing about numbers. Set explicit success criteria now — p99 latency under 250ms at current peak load, and fleet utilisation above 80% — and commit to revisiting the purchase decision at the end of that window with real data. If we hit those targets, we likely defer or shrink the purchase. If we miss them, we will have a much sharper case for exactly how many nodes we need, which is a better procurement argument than we have today.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be clear about what we do not know. Demand forecasts for the new search feature are soft, and if adoption outpaces expectations, utilisation work will buy us time but not capacity, and we should be prepared to move quickly on procurement — lead times on A100-class hardware are currently 10–14 weeks, so we should pre-qualify a vendor now even if we do not order. There is also execution risk: the engineers who would do this work are the same ones carrying the on-call load, and slippage is plausible. I would rather discover that in eight weeks than discover it after the purchase order is signed.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.

Let's start with the case that's easiest to feel: our utilisation numbers. Across our inference fleet, average GPU utilisation sits somewhere in the low thirties, with peaks that occasionally saturate a node and long troughs overnight and on weekends. That gap between average and peak is exactly the kind of thing that makes "buy more" look wasteful on paper. If we can lift average utilisation into the fifties through better batching, smarter scheduling, and consolidating the long tail of small workloads onto shared nodes, we effectively add capacity without spending a dollar on silicon. The engineering effort is real but bounded — mostly queueing logic, a proper job scheduler, and some unglamorous work on model placement. It's also fast: we could see meaningful improvements within a month, whereas hardware procurement, even expedited, is a two-to-three-month lead time before a single token gets served.

But utilisation gains have a ceiling, and it's important to be honest about where that ceiling is. Some of our low utilisation is structural, not operational. Our latency-sensitive serving workloads need headroom to absorb traffic spikes; a GPU running at 85% average is a GPU that starts queueing requests during the afternoon peak, and queueing means p95 latency degrades exactly when users are most active. We've already had two incidents this quarter where response times crept past our SLO because a batch job and a traffic spike collided. Squeezing utilisation harder on latency-critical paths trades reliability for efficiency, and that's a trade we've historically regretted. So the realistic target isn't "fill every GPU to the brim" — it's something like a 40–50% improvement in effective throughput on batch and offline work, while leaving serving capacity deliberately underutilised.

Now the cost side. The hardware we'd buy — another two nodes of the class we currently run — is roughly $180K all-in, plus the ongoing power, cooling, and the very real cost of someone racking and maintaining it. That's not catastrophic for our budget, but it's not trivial either, and it's worth asking what else that money could do. The opportunity cost argument cuts both ways, though. The engineering time to improve utilisation is maybe two engineers for six weeks — time that won't go toward the product roadmap. If the utilisation project slips or underdelivers, we've burned a quarter of capacity planning and still need the hardware, having paid for the delay twice. Buying hardware is the more expensive path but the lower-variance one.
